title: On the Moon, a hammer and a feather hit the ground together

cover.alt: David Scott on the Moon beside the Apollo 15 lunar module, holding a hammer and a feather.

body: Without air resistance, gravity accelerates everything at the same rate, whatever its mass. In 1971 Apollo 15 commander David Scott tested this on camera, dropping a hammer and a falcon feather side by side on the airless Moon; they landed at the same moment. Galileo is often said to have proved the same thing by dropping balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa, but most historians think that was a thought experiment, not a real test.

slides.alt: Apollo 15 commander David Scott stands beside the lunar module on the Moon, holds up a hammer and a feather, and lets them fall together.
slides.caption: Apollo 15, 1971: David Scott lets go of a hammer and a falcon feather at the same moment, and they hit the ground together.

slides.heading: How hard gravity pulls at the surface
slides.note: About a sixth of Earth’s pull on the Moon; Jupiter’s figure is taken at its cloud tops
slides.explanation: A slower fall on the Moon, but the same for hammer and feather: with no air, everything accelerates alike.

slides.question: Why did the hammer and the feather land at the same moment?
options: No air, so nothing slowed the feather
The feather was weighted with lead
slides.explanation: Without air resistance, gravity accelerates everything at the same rate whatever its mass. Apollo 15’s David Scott showed it on camera in 1971.

slides.heading: Fact or myth?

items.text: Air resistance is what slows a falling feather on Earth
The Moon has no gravity, so things just drift
Apollo 15’s David Scott did the test on camera in 1971
Galileo’s Pisa drop was probably only a thought experiment

slides.explanation: Gravity accelerates everything at the same rate; only air resistance separates a feather from a hammer. The Moon’s gravity is about a sixth of Earth’s.
